A disclaimer buried in the repo root doesn't offset an unqualified assurance claim sitting in the README hero and CLI banner — the two places users form their expectations before ever finding DISCLAIMER.md. [...] "SOC2-ready" | Not marketing puffery — it's a specific compliance-readiness claim. If you haven't gone through a SOC2 Type I/II audit or engaged an auditor, this is a false compliance claim, not tone. [...] "battle-tested for compliance-critical environments" | Implies a proven track record in regulated deployments. Do you have evidence (named customers, audit logs, incident history) or is this aspirational?

The disclaimer-elsewhere argument doesn't hold. MIT's warranty disclaimer protects you legally for warranty purposes, but it doesn't retroactively neutralize an affirmative claim made in the hero section or `--help` banner. Users form their trust expectations from the first thing they read — that's exactly where the boundary needs to live, not buried in a separate file they may never open. [And separately:] "SOC2-ready" is a specific compliance claim...this is a factual claim you can't support. "Battle-tested for compliance-critical environments" and "trusted by teams running regulated workloads" assert real-world validation and adoption in regulated settings. If you can't point to specific evidence...this is an unsupported fitness claim.

Why a boilerplate MIT disclaimer elsewhere doesn't help: an "AS IS, no warranty" disclaimer limits liability for how the software *performs*; it does nothing to excuse false statements about what the software *is* or *has been certified as*... a disclaimer buried in a separate file that most readers won't see before reading your hero pitch materially weakens any argument that it was disclosed. ... Drop "SOC2-ready" entirely unless you have an actual SOC 2 report... Drop "battle-tested for compliance-critical environments" unless you can point to real production usage in such environments.
